\begin{abstract}
We develop a self-contained dictionary among stable extensions of abstract argumentation frameworks, kernels of directed graphs, and P-position solutions of normal-play games. Reversing an attack relation converts stability exactly into the kernel property, while the kernel axioms are equivalent to the recursive condition that a position is losing precisely when all its options are non-losing. Terminal positions consequently belong to every kernel. The directed three-cycle has no solution in any of the three senses, whereas the directed four-cycle has two distinct alternating stable extensions. For well-founded move relations, recursive evaluation constructs a kernel and well-founded induction proves it unique. Thus every terminating normal-play game has a unique P-position solution, and every well-founded argumentation framework has a unique stable extension. We also describe finite algorithms, applications, and extensions toward cycle classification, grounded semantics, and Sprague--Grundy theory.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
Directed relations appear under different names across mathematics. In abstract argumentation an arrow records that one argument attacks another. In directed graph theory, arrows determine independent and absorbing sets called kernels. In combinatorial game theory, arrows are legal moves, and one seeks positions that are losing under normal play. The definitions are close, but their arrow conventions conceal an exact identification.

The central observation is that reversal resolves this discrepancy. A stable extension attacks every excluded argument, whereas every vertex excluded from a kernel points toward that kernel. Thus stability for a relation is kernelhood for its transpose. The two kernel axioms, in turn, combine into the game recursion: a position belongs to the kernel if and only if all legal options lie outside it.

This translation reveals a common obstruction and a common determinacy principle. The directed triangle has no stable extension, kernel, or consistent P-position labeling. The directed square instead has two alternating solutions, showing that cyclicity may cause either nonexistence or nonuniqueness. If play cannot continue indefinitely, recursive evaluation is legitimate, constructs a kernel, and supplies the induction that makes it unique.

Our structural statements apply to arbitrary sets and require neither finiteness nor decidability. Finiteness enters only in the explicit algorithms of Section~\ref{sec:algorithms}.

\section{Relations, kernels, and stable extensions}
Let $X$ be a set and let $R\subseteq X\times X$ be a binary relation. We write $R(x,y)$ or $x\to y$ for an arrow from $x$ to $y$.

\begin{definition}[Reversal]
The opposite relation $R^{\mathrm{op}}$ is defined by
\[
R^{\mathrm{op}}(x,y)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad R(y,x).
\]
Clearly $(R^{\mathrm{op}})^{\mathrm{op}}=R$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Kernel]
A subset $K\subseteq X$ is a \emph{kernel} of $R$ if it is both independent and absorbing. Independence means
\[
\forall x,y\in K,\qquad \neg R(x,y),
\]
and absorption means
\[
\forall x\notin K,\qquad \exists y\in K\text{ such that }R(x,y).
\]
\end{definition}

The word kernel here denotes the directed-graph concept rather than the null space of a linear map. Independence is an internal prohibition, while absorption is an external coverage condition.

Now interpret $R(x,y)$ as saying that argument $x$ attacks argument $y$.

\begin{definition}[Stable extension]
A subset $S\subseteq X$ is \emph{stable} for $R$ if it is conflict-free,
\[
\forall x,y\in S,\qquad \neg R(x,y),
\]
and attacks every excluded argument,
\[
\forall x\notin S,\qquad \exists y\in S\text{ such that }R(y,x).
\]
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Stable--kernel equivalence]\label{thm:stablekernel}
For every relation $R$ and subset $S\subseteq X$,
\[
S\text{ is stable for }R
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
S\text{ is a kernel of }R^{\mathrm{op}}.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Conflict-freeness is invariant under reversal: an arrow between two selected vertices remains internal after its direction is reversed. For an excluded $x$, the existence of $y\in S$ satisfying $R(y,x)$ is exactly the existence of $y\in S$ satisfying $R^{\mathrm{op}}(x,y)$. Hence stable coverage for $R$ is absorption for $R^{\mathrm{op}}$, and the two pairs of defining conditions coincide.
\end{proof}

No acyclicity or finiteness assumption is involved; the result is a direct equality of concepts after reversing arrows.

\section{Normal-play solutions}
Interpret $R(x,y)$ as a legal move from $x$ to $y$. A P-position is losing for the player about to move, while an N-position is winning for that player.

\begin{definition}[P-position solution]
A subset $P\subseteq X$ is a game solution for $R$ if, for every $x\in X$,
\[
x\in P
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\forall y\in X,\ R(x,y)\Longrightarrow y\notin P.
\]
\end{definition}

The forward implication says that no move joins two P-positions. The reverse implication, read contrapositively, says that every position outside $P$ has a move into $P$.

\begin{theorem}[Kernel--game equivalence]\label{thm:kernelgame}
A subset $P\subseteq X$ is a kernel of $R$ if and only if it is a P-position solution for $R$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Suppose $P$ is a kernel. If $x\in P$, independence places every successor outside $P$. Conversely, if all successors of $x$ lie outside $P$ but $x\notin P$, absorption supplies a successor in $P$, a contradiction. Thus the required biconditional holds.

Conversely, assume the biconditional. If $x,y\in P$ and $R(x,y)$, its forward direction at $x$ implies $y\notin P$, proving independence. If $x\notin P$, the right side must be false, so some successor of $x$ belongs to $P$. This is absorption.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Three-way dictionary]\label{cor:dictionary}
For an attack relation $R$ and $S\subseteq X$, the following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item $S$ is stable for $R$;
\item $S$ is a kernel of $R^{\mathrm{op}}$;
\item $S$ is a P-position solution of the reversed-arrow game $R^{\mathrm{op}}$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{corollary}

\begin{definition}[Terminal position]
A position $t$ is terminal if $\neg R(t,y)$ for every $y\in X$.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[Terminal-position principle]\label{prop:terminal}
Every terminal position belongs to every kernel and hence to every P-position solution.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
If a terminal $t$ lay outside a kernel $K$, absorption would produce $y\in K$ with $R(t,y)$, contradicting terminality.
\end{proof}

Thus the normal-play rule that a player with no move loses is not an additional convention once independence and absorption are imposed. The directed geometry forces the boundary condition.

\section{Cycles: obstruction and multiplicity}
Let $C_3$ be the relation on $\{0,1,2\}$ given by
\[
0\to1,\qquad 1\to2,\qquad 2\to0.
\]

\begin{theorem}[Odd triangle obstruction]\label{thm:c3}
The directed three-cycle has no kernel. Consequently it has no stable extension and no consistent P-position solution.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The empty set is not absorbing. If a kernel is nonempty, cyclic symmetry lets us suppose that it contains $0$. Independence excludes $1$. Since $1$ has only the successor $2$, absorption forces $2$ into the kernel. But $2\to0$ then violates independence. Thus no kernel exists. Reversal produces another directed triangle, so Theorems~\ref{thm:stablekernel} and~\ref{thm:kernelgame} give the other two claims.
\end{proof}

The game contradiction can be read as failed alternation: if $0$ is P, then $2$ is N, then $1$ is P, forcing $0$ to be N. An odd number of negations cannot close consistently around the cycle.

Now let $C_4$ be the relation on $\{0,1,2,3\}$ given by
\[
0\to1\to2\to3\to0.
\]

\begin{proposition}[Alternating kernel]
The set $\{0,2\}$ is a kernel of $C_4$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
There is no arrow between $0$ and $2$. The excluded vertex $1$ points to $2$, and the excluded vertex $3$ points to $0$. Thus the set is independent and absorbing.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Two stable extensions of the square]\label{thm:c4}
The directed four-cycle has two distinct stable extensions,
\[
\{0,2\}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\{1,3\}.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Each alternating pair is conflict-free. Every excluded vertex is attacked by the preceding selected vertex, so both pairs satisfy stable coverage. They are distinct because $0$ belongs only to the first.
\end{proof}

The square shows that existence need not imply uniqueness. Alternating labels close consistently around an even cycle, but they admit two phases.

\section{Well-founded recursion and unique kernels}
Cycles make recursive outcome definitions circular. We remove this problem by requiring that play terminate.

\begin{definition}[Well-founded move relation]
A move relation $R$ is well-founded for backward induction if there is no infinite sequence
\[
x_0\to x_1\to x_2\to\cdots.
\]
Equivalently, every nonempty set of positions contains one with no successor in that set. On a finite graph this is equivalent to acyclicity.
\end{definition}

For well-founded $R$, define a predicate $L$ recursively by
\begin{equation}\label{eq:loss}
L(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\forall y,\ R(x,y)\Longrightarrow\neg L(y).
\end{equation}
Its value at $x$ depends only on positions later in play, so well-founded recursion defines it without circularity, even on infinite sets.

\begin{lemma}[Losing-position equation]
The recursively defined predicate $L$ satisfies Equation~\eqref{eq:loss} at every position.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
This is the defining unfolding equation for recursion over a well-founded relation.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Existence of a well-founded kernel]\label{thm:existence}
If $R$ is well-founded, then $K_L=\{x\in X:L(x)\}$ is a kernel of $R$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
If $x\in K_L$ and $R(x,y)$, Equation~\eqref{eq:loss} gives $y\notin K_L$, proving independence. If $x\notin K_L$, the universal statement on the right of Equation~\eqref{eq:loss} is false. Hence some successor $y$ satisfies $L(y)$, proving absorption.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Uniqueness under well-foundedness]\label{thm:uniqueness}
A well-founded directed relation has at most one kernel.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Let $K$ and $M$ be kernels. Use well-founded induction on $x$, assuming membership in $K$ and $M$ agrees for every successor of $x$. If $x\in K$ but $x\notin M$, absorption for $M$ gives a successor $y\in M$. The induction hypothesis puts $y$ in $K$, contradicting independence of $K$. The case $x\in M$ but $x\notin K$ is symmetric. Thus membership agrees at $x$, and induction gives $K=M$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Unique kernel theorem]\label{thm:uniquekernel}
Every well-founded directed graph has exactly one kernel, namely the recursively defined set $K_L$ of losing positions.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Combine Theorems~\ref{thm:existence} and~\ref{thm:uniqueness}.
\end{proof}

\section{Determinacy and stable semantics}
\begin{theorem}[Determinacy of terminating normal-play games]\label{thm:game}
Every normal-play game with no infinite play has exactly one P-position solution. A position belongs to it precisely when all legal options lie outside it.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The move relation has a unique kernel by Theorem~\ref{thm:uniquekernel}; kernels are exactly P-position solutions by Theorem~\ref{thm:kernelgame}.
\end{proof}

The theorem also supplies a positional strategy. From every N-position, absorption gives a move to a P-position; from a P-position, every move goes to an N-position.

For argumentation, orientation must be stated carefully.

\begin{definition}[Well-founded attack framework]
An attack relation $A$ is well-founded if there is no infinite backward attack chain
\[
x_0\leftarrow x_1\leftarrow x_2\leftarrow\cdots,
\]
or, equivalently, if $A^{\mathrm{op}}$ is a well-founded move relation.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Unique stable extension]\label{thm:stableunique}
Every well-founded attack framework has exactly one stable extension.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The reversed relation $A^{\mathrm{op}}$ has a unique kernel by Theorem~\ref{thm:uniquekernel}. Theorem~\ref{thm:stablekernel} identifies that kernel with the unique stable extension of $A$.
\end{proof}

The triangle and square show that well-foundedness has genuine content: without it, existence may fail or uniqueness may fail.

\section{Algorithms}\label{sec:algorithms}
For a finite acyclic move graph, compute a topological ordering and process vertices in reverse order. Label a vertex P when all successors are already labeled N; otherwise label it N and retain one P-successor as a winning move. The P-vertices form the unique kernel by Theorem~\ref{thm:uniquekernel}. With adjacency lists, topological sorting and evaluation use $O(|X|+|R|)$ time and storage.

For small cyclic graphs, exhaustive enumeration offers a transparent alternative. Test every subset $K\subseteq X$. Reject it if an edge has both endpoints in $K$ or if an excluded vertex has no edge into $K$. A straightforward implementation takes $O(2^{|X|}(|X|+|R|))$ time and linear auxiliary space beyond its output. This procedure finds no kernel on $C_3$ and the two alternating kernels on $C_4$.

Stable extensions may be enumerated directly by testing conflict-freeness and outward attack coverage, or indirectly by reversing all edges and enumerating kernels. The latter makes Corollary~\ref{cor:dictionary} computationally operational.

\section{Applications and discussion}
In structured debate, an attack graph can model incompatible claims, legal arguments, diagnoses, or policy proposals. A stable extension is a coherent accepted set that rebuts every rejected item. Under well-foundedness, backward evaluation yields a unique verdict together with explanation chains: every exclusion is defeated by an inclusion.

In games and planning systems, the kernel marks states from which no move preserves membership. Every non-kernel state has a transition into the kernel. This gives a strategy and classifies terminal states without a special computational case, as Proposition~\ref{prop:terminal} already forces their status.

In dependency networks, a kernel selects mutually noninteracting representatives while ensuring that each unselected vertex delegates to one selected vertex. Acyclic workflows yield a unique selection; cyclic dependencies warn that the selection may be absent or ambiguous.

Three structural regimes emerge. Odd cyclic feedback can make local rules globally inconsistent. Even cyclic feedback can support several coherent global phases. Well-foundedness removes circular dependence, enabling both recursive construction and inductive comparison. The bridge transfers techniques accordingly: game recursion constructs graph kernels, graph obstructions explain failures of stable semantics, and argumentation language interprets multiple game solutions as competing coherent positions.

\section{Future directions}
A first goal is a uniform classification of directed cycles: positive even cycles should have exactly two alternating kernels, while odd cycles should have none. This would place Theorems~\ref{thm:c3} and~\ref{thm:c4} inside a complete parity theorem.

A second direction is kernel-perfectness, beginning with finite acyclic digraphs and proceeding toward hereditary conditions such as exclusion of odd directed cycles. A third is to compare the recursively defined stable extension with grounded semantics; in the well-founded case, one expects equality with the least fixed point of the characteristic defense operator.

A fourth direction enriches the Boolean predicate $L$ to a Sprague--Grundy value
\[
g(x)=\operatorname{mex}\{g(y):R(x,y)\},
\]
where $\operatorname{mex}$ is the least excluded nonnegative integer. Zero-value positions should be exactly the kernel, while nim-addition should describe disjunctive sums. Algorithmic extensions include output-sensitive enumeration, compact certificates of nonexistence, and dynamic updates after adding or deleting arrows.

\section{Conclusion}
Stable argumentation, directed kernels, and normal-play P-positions share an exact mathematical core. Reversing attacks turns stable extensions into kernels, and kernelhood is equivalent to the recursive losing-position equation. Terminal positions are necessarily losing. The directed triangle demonstrates nonexistence, while the directed square demonstrates multiplicity. Well-foundedness removes both pathologies: recursion constructs a kernel and induction proves it unique. One theorem therefore expresses determinacy for terminating games, unique kernel existence for well-founded digraphs, and unique stable semantics for well-founded argumentation frameworks.

from itertools import combinations
from typing import Iterable, TypeVar

def powerset(vertices: Iterable[int]) -> Iterable[frozenset[int]]:
    """Yield every subset of a finite collection of vertices."""
    items = tuple(vertices)
    for size in range(len(items) + 1):
        for chosen in combinations(items, size):

def is_kernel(vertices: set[int], edges: set[Edge], candidate: frozenset[int]) -> bool:
    """Test directed independence and absorption."""
    independent = all(not (u in candidate and v in candidate) for u, v in edges)
    absorbing = all(
        x in candidate or any(u == x and v in candidate for u, v in edges)
        for x in vertices
    )
    return independent and absorbing


def is_stable(vertices: set[int], attacks: set[Edge], candidate: frozenset[int]) -> bool:
    """Test conflict-freeness and outward attack of every excluded vertex."""
    conflict_free = all(not (u in candidate and v in candidate) for u, v in attacks)
    covers_outside = all(
        x in candidate or any(u in candidate and v == x for u, v in attacks)
        for x in vertices
    )
    return conflict_free and covers_outside


def is_game_solution(vertices: set[int], moves: set[Edge], p_positions: frozenset[int]) -> bool:
    """Test x in P iff every move from x ends outside P."""
    return all(
        (x in p_positions)
        == all(v not in p_positions for u, v in moves if u == x)
        for x in vertices
    )


def enumerate_kernels(vertices: set[int], edges: set[Edge]) -> list[frozenset[int]]:
    """Enumerate all kernels by exhaustive subset testing."""
    return [candidate for candidate in powerset(vertices) if is_kernel(vertices, edges, candidate)]


def enumerate_stable(vertices: set[int], attacks: set[Edge]) -> list[frozenset[int]]:
    """Enumerate all stable extensions by exhaustive subset testing."""
    return [candidate for candidate in powerset(vertices) if is_stable(vertices, attacks, candidate)]


def backward_kernel(vertices: set[int], moves: set[Edge]) -> frozenset[int]:
    """Compute the unique kernel of a finite acyclic move graph in linear time."""
    successors: dict[int, list[int]] = {v: [] for v in vertices}
    indegree: dict[int, int] = {v: 0 for v in vertices}
    for source, target in moves:
        successors[source].append(target)
        indegree[target] += 1

    queue = deque(v for v in vertices if indegree[v] == 0)
    topological: list[int] = []
    while queue:
        source = queue.popleft()
        topological.append(source)
        for target in successors[source]:
            indegree[target] -= 1
            if indegree[target] == 0:

        raise ValueError("backward_kernel requires an acyclic graph")

    for source in reversed(topological):
        if all(target not in losing for target in successors[source]):

    if length < 2:

    vertices = set(range(length))
    return vertices, {(i, (i + 1) % length) for i in vertices}

concept.concept_description: Zero-knowledge proofs let you convince someone a statement is true without revealing WHY. Apply this to mathematics: a zero-knowledge proof of a theorem T convinces the verifier that T is provable in PA without revealing any step of the proof. Conjecture: Every theorem provable in Peano Arithmetic has a zero-knowledge proof whose communication complexity is polynomial in the length of the theorem statement (not the proof). This follows from the PCP theorem combined with the fact that PA-proofs can be arithmetized. The zero-knowledge protocol: (1) Prover commits to each proof step using a collision-resistant hash. (2) Verifier randomly challenges one proof step. (3) Prover opens that step and shows it follows from the axioms. Repeating O(k) times gives soundness error 2^{-k}. The proof is zero-knowledge because the verifier only sees one random step per challenge. Test: implement a zero-knowledge proof system for propositional tautologies and prove that a verifier learns nothing beyond the validity of the tautology. Impact: mathematicians can certify results without revealing their methods — a mathematical equivalent of sealed-bid auctions for proof strategies.

namespace AdjointBlochKato

/-- A linearized global deformation problem: parameters are constrained by a relation map,
and admissible first-order deformations form its kernel. -/
structure DeformationPresentation (K : Type*) [Field K] where
  Parameters : Type*
  Obstructions : Type*
  parametersAddCommGroup : AddCommGroup Parameters
  parametersModule : Module K Parameters
  obstructionsAddCommGroup : AddCommGroup Obstructions
  obstructionsModule : Module K Obstructions
  relations : Parameters →ₗ[K] Obstructions

attribute [instance] DeformationPresentation.parametersAddCommGroup
  DeformationPresentation.parametersModule DeformationPresentation.obstructionsAddCommGroup
  DeformationPresentation.obstructionsModule

/-- The tangent space cut out by the linearized global and local conditions. -/
abbrev DeformationPresentation.tangent {K : Type*} [Field K]
    (P : DeformationPresentation K) : Submodule K P.Parameters := P.relations.ker

/-- Rigidity means that the deformation problem has no nonzero first-order deformation. -/
def DeformationPresentation.Rigid {K : Type*} [Field K]
    (P : DeformationPresentation K) : Prop := P.tangent = ⊥

/-- Vanishing of the tangent space is exactly injectivity of the linearized relation map. -/
theorem rigid_iff_injective {K : Type*} [Field K] (P : DeformationPresentation K) :
    P.Rigid ↔ Function.Injective P.relations := by
  unfold DeformationPresentation.Rigid DeformationPresentation.tangent
  exact LinearMap.ker_eq_bot
